title: Complement closure of conjunctive languages
formal: For every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every conjunctive grammar G over it, does there exist a conjunctive grammar H over the same terminal alphabet with \[L(H)=\Sigma^*\setminus L(G)\,?\]
definitions: A conjunctive grammar has a finite terminal alphabet Sigma, a disjoint finite set N of nonterminals, a start symbol S, and finitely many rules A→alpha_1 & … & alpha_k, with k≥1 and alpha_i∈(Sigma∪N)*. Interpret a terminal as its singleton language, a word of symbols as concatenation of their languages, a conjunction as intersection, and alternative rules for A as union. The language tuple is the least fixed point of these monotone equations, equivalently the union of their iterations starting with empty nonterminal languages. An empty right-hand-side word denotes {epsilon}; a nonterminal with no rules denotes the empty language. No negation appears in the grammar. The complement is relative to all finite words over the declared alphabet, including the empty word. H may use arbitrarily many new nonterminals and rules. The target is closure of the language class: no computable transformation, grammar-size bound, linearity or unambiguity requirement is added. Boolean grammars may use negation and have different semantic issues; their complement properties do not provide a conjunctive grammar automatically. Linear conjunctive grammars restrict each conjunct to at most one nonterminal and are not the full class in this question.
answer_criterion: Prove the closure statement in Lean, with an equivalent conjunctive grammar for every input language, or give a conjunctive grammar and prove that its complement has no conjunctive grammar whatsoever. Showing that a complement is not context-free, not linear, or not unambiguous does not prove non-closure of the full conjunctive class.
context:
Okhotin’s survey treats conjunction as an extension of context-free syntax and distinguishes it from grammars with explicit negation. The complement question concerns the expressive power of conjunction alone.

The Martynova–Okhotin non-closure result concerns unambiguous linear context-free languages. Its conclusion is not a separation for unrestricted conjunctive grammars.
why: This asks whether grammar conjunction and recursion can express negation without an explicit negation operation.

This asks whether conjunction and ordinary grammar recursion can express negation without adding the explicit negation operator of Boolean grammars.
